top.title: Uh oh, tokens are getting too expensive...
top.description:
AI tokens are cheaper than ever. So why are companies suddenly panicking about how much they’re spending on AI? Over the past year, companies pushed employees to use AI as much as possible. Engineers got access to tools like Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, and a growing list of AI agents. Some companies even turned usage into a goal. The result was a wave of “tokenmaxxing,” where more AI use was treated like more progress. But that did not always happen. Uber blew through its AI budget in 4 months. Meta workers reportedly used tens of trillions of tokens in a month. Amazon had an internal AI leaderboard that employees started gaming. And across the industry, companies are realizing that more tokens does not always mean better work. The weird part is that token prices have dropped a lot since 2023. But AI tools now think longer, loop through more steps, reread more context, and handle more complex tasks. That means usage can explode even when each token gets cheaper. This is the strange economics of AI right now. Cheaper tokens created more demand. More demand created higher bills. And now the entire AI market is shifting from simple subscriptions to usage-based pricing.

top.title: Upwork Is (Finally) Getting What They Deserve…
top.description:
Upwork helped define the modern freelance economy. For years it connected millions of businesses with designers, developers, writers, and creators around the world. But after becoming one of the biggest freelance platforms on the internet, things started to change. In this video, we take a look at how Upwork slowly lost the trust of the very people who built the platform. From rising commissions and paid Connects to hidden pricing algorithms and contract fees, each change promised to improve the marketplace. Instead, many freelancers felt they were paying more while getting less in return. At the same time, competition exploded. New freelance platforms entered the market with simpler pricing, remote work growth slowed after the pandemic, and AI began cutting into many of the entry level jobs that once fueled Upwork's growth. Revenue has stalled, the company has gone through major layoffs, and investors are no longer betting on the same future they once were. So how did one of the biggest freelance marketplaces end up here? And can it recover before more freelancers decide to leave? This is the rise and fall of Upwork.

top.title: Klarna Is (Finally) Getting What They Deserve...
top.description:
Klarna was supposed to be one of the biggest fintech success stories of the decade. The company helped popularize Buy Now, Pay Later and built a business around letting consumers split purchases into smaller payments. By 2025, it had more than 100 million active users, growing revenue, and a blockbuster IPO that valued the company at over $17 billion. But behind the growth, serious cracks were beginning to show. In this video, we take a look at how Klarna's core business model works, why rising credit losses are becoming a major problem, and how the company may have fallen into its own debt trap. While Klarna pays merchants upfront, it still needs customers to repay those loans. As more borrowers fall behind, the cost of funding that debt continues to rise. We also explore Klarna's dramatic shift from Buy Now, Pay Later into something much bigger: a digital banking platform. From debit cards and long-term financing products to its partnership with Walmart and OnePay, Klarna is trying to reinvent itself before investors lose confidence. The question is whether that strategy is actually working. Despite strong revenue growth and a successful IPO, profits remain elusive, the stock has fallen sharply, and the company is now facing a shareholder lawsuit that claims investors were misled about credit risks. Klarna's story may no longer be about Buy Now, Pay Later. It may be about whether Wall Street bought into a vision that never truly existed.

top.title: No One Is Using Bumble...
top.description:
Bumble was once one of the biggest success stories in tech. It grew to 58 million users, generated over a billion dollars in revenue, and reached a staggering $14 billion valuation after its IPO. Today, the stock is down roughly 95%. So what went wrong? The story starts with founder Whitney Wolfe Herd, who helped build Tinder before leaving the company and launching Bumble with a simple but powerful idea: women make the first move. That one feature helped Bumble stand out in a crowded market and fueled years of explosive growth. But after going public in 2021, things began to change. Major shareholders started cashing out, growth slowed, and the entire online dating industry entered a downturn. Downloads fell, younger users became less interested in dating apps, and burnout started spreading across nearly every platform. Bumble's response only made things more complicated. New leadership introduced major changes, including features that moved the app closer to Tinder and weakened the very identity that made Bumble unique in the first place. Users noticed, and many weren't happy. Now, with declining revenue, layoffs, and growing competition from Hinge, Bumble is attempting another reinvention. This time the company is betting on AI matchmaking instead of endless swiping. Can Bumble pull off a turnaround, or is this another example of a tech company losing sight of what made it successful? This is the rise, fall, and uncertain future of Bumble.
